newsitem.title: USA: Powerful storm pounds Western U.S.
newsitem.headline: Powerful storm pounds Western U.S.

text.p: A fierce storm made its way over the Pacific Northwest on Sunday, dumping heavy rain, ice and snow on a region still reeling from last week's punishing cold front.
Power was cut off to part of the Portland International Airport for a few hours during the early morning rush, causing dozens of flight delays, schedule changes and cancellations.

"It impacted a lot of people trying to leave Portland," said Darrel Buttice, spokesman for the airport, "It's going to take a considerable number of hours before it's back to normal for those airlines that are impacted."
For motorists, travel was restricted on several major roadways in Oregon and Washington state due to snow and ice.

Flood and storm warnings have been issued from northern California, where more than 10 inches (25 cm) of rainfall was expected, to northern Washington, where 10 inches (25 cm) or more of new snow was in the forecast.

The storm has knocked out power to thousands in Washington state, Oregon and California, and has set back efforts to restore electricity to homes and businesses that were cut off by the ice and snow storm that struck on Thursday and Friday.
Puget Sound Power and Light Co., which services nine counties in western Washington state, said the new storm was responsible for scattered power outages across its territory.

Early on Sunday, Puget Power said 55,000 of its customers were without power, down from a peak of nearly 250,000 on Friday. But new outages were reported later, lifting the number of its customers without electricity to about 80,000.
"It's beginning to climb back up," said Puget Power spokeswoman Kristen Wappler, but added, "These are extreme conditions. There could be many new outages."
Puget Power said 185 of its repair crews were racing to restore electricity to those affected. Fresh crews were being brought in from as far south as Los Angeles.

A winter storm warning was in effect for much of Washington state. Parts of Washington experienced freezing rain mixed with snow. By Sunday night, northern Washington could receive three to 10 inches of new snow, while eight to 12 inches were forecast for the Cascades.

Across the state, major roadways were closed due to compact snow, ice and freezing rain. Blizzard conditions were reported north of Seattle to the border, restricting travel on Interstate 5. Several passes over the Cascades were also closed, the Washington State Patrol said.
In Oregon, about 20,000 Portland General Electric Co. customers remained without electricity following Thursday's ice storm, down from a peak of 130,000 on Friday.
Portland General Electric spokeswoman Vickie Rocker said 220 crews were trying to restore power to homes and businesses, but warned the weather was hampering their efforts.

Freezing rain was falling in the Portland area, causing new power outages as tree limbs, heavy with ice, crashed down, taking power lines with them. "There's about an inch of ice on everything," said Craig Schmidt, a forecaster with the National Weather Service in Portland.
Lowland flooding was reported in northwest Oregon, and all of western Oregon's rivers were under a flood watch. More severe flooding was forecast for later Sunday and Monday.

Flood watches were declared for most of northern California, where the heaviest rain was expected. The National Weather Service issued flood warnings for the Russian and Napa rivers, which were expected to rise above flood stage on Sunday afternoon and night.

Thousands of people living close to the Russian River were preparing for the worst, said Chris Godley, assistant coordinator of the Sonoma County emergency services department. Some residents were stacking sandbags to protect their homes.

In northern California, winds could reach 35 to 45 mph (55 to 70 kph) with gusts to 60 mph (95 kph) in lower elevations, and wind bursts to well over 100 mph (160 kph) over the highest ridges of the Sierra Nevada.
Wind damage has already been reported in Eureka, California, and strong gusts were recorded in the Sierras.
Pacific Gas & Electric Co. said about 6,800 of its customers have lost power in the storm thus far, mostly along California's north coast. Power was quickly restored to most of them.
